surface: public.user_roles RLS: 'Deny all deletes to user_roles' is a PERMISSIVE no-op
claim: user_roles carries a policy named 'Deny all deletes to user_roles' with USING (false), but it is declared PERMISSIVE, not RESTRICTIVE. Permissive policies are OR-ed together, so a permissive USING(false) contributes nothing at all: it can never subtract access. DELETE on user_roles is therefore governed entirely by the sibling 'Admins can delete roles' policy, exactly as if the deny policy did not exist. The current net behaviour is probably the intended one (admins may delete roles), so this is not an open hole -- it is a security control that reads as a hard stop, is named as a hard stop, and enforces nothing. That is the 'configured but does nothing' class, and on the table that grants admin. Note the contrast with its twin: 'Deny all updates to user_roles' is also permissive-false, but it happens to be the ONLY permissive UPDATE policy on the table, so updates really are denied -- by the absence of any passing policy, not by the deny. Two policies written the same way, one working by accident and one inert. Routed to lh-authz-rls as the owning lane.

claim: The hook reads as an either/or and behaves as a both: on NATIVE it attaches the Capacitor Keyboard listeners AND the visualViewport listeners at the same time. claim: THE FOUR CRON DETECTORS DO NOT DUPLICATE EACH OTHER — but sweep_dead_crons is the sole watcher of the other three and has no watcher of its own. Answering the orchestrator's question directly: there is NO overlap. The four read different inputs, emit different verdicts, write different error_logs sources, and are deliberately staggered. sweep_cron_http_failures (*/15) reads net._http_response status codes and catches an edge function answering non-2xx -> 'cron-http'. sweep_silent_cron_failures (:47) reads cron_run_log bodies against cron_work_expectations.candidate_key and catches a 2xx that found candidates and dispositioned none -> 'cron-silent'. sweep_dead_crons (:53) reads cron.job_run_details against expected_max_gap and catches unscheduled / inactive / never-ran / dead / erroring -> 'cron-dead'. sweep_cron_blackouts (:57) differences the AGGREGATE cron.job_run_details dispatch stream for holes >15 minutes and catches pg_cron itself dispatching nothing -> 'cron-blackout'. Four distinct failure modes, no redundancy. THE REAL RISK IS TOPOLOGICAL, NOT DUPLICATION. All four detectors are themselves pg_cron jobs, and only ONE thing can notice a detector failing: sweep_dead_crons, which is the only function in the entire 254-function catalog besides the read-only reporter cron_dispatch_health() that reads expected_max_gap. So sweep_dead_crons watches the other three — and nothing watches sweep_dead_crons. If it stops firing or starts raising, the database emits no signal of any kind, and the failure of every other detector becomes simultaneously unobservable. Compounding it, sweep_dead_crons is blind to intermittent failure (CJ-004), which is the LIVE state of sweep_silent_cron_failures: 3 raises, 0 cron-dead rows.
